scope.start: 10a: R. Shimon's baraita that meat cooked in milk is permitted in benefit (opens mid-exchange on why he counts meat in milk as food)
scope.end: 10b: the derivation of 'you shall redeem': immediately and for any amount, unlike the firstborn son

sections.title: Meat in Milk as Food: Permitted in Benefit, and Once Fit to Eat
sections.gist: Continuing the question of why R. Shimon counts meat cooked in milk as food: he holds it is permitted in benefit, and the baraita gives that reason and adds a second, that it was once fit to eat.

bullets.text: R. Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of R. Shimon: meat cooked in milk is forbidden to eat but permitted in benefit.

The source links "a holy people" said of meat in milk (Devarim 14:21) with "holy men" said of *tereifah* (Shemot 22:30). *Tereifah* is forbidden to eat but permitted in benefit, so the same holds for meat cooked in milk.
The practical case is pet food containing meat cooked with milk. The accepted ruling follows the majority, for whom *basar be'chalav* is *asur be'hana'ah*, but R. Shimon's dissent is on record.

Answer: the baraita states one reason and adds another. It is food that can be fed to others (gentiles). And even for a Jew it had a time when it was fit to eat, before the meat and milk were cooked together.

Each reason is enough alone. The other items on R. Shimon's list meet neither: they can't be given to gentiles, and they were never actually food beforehand. An *eglah arufah* was never food the way separate meat and milk were.

sections.title: Peter Chamor After Arifah: Rava's Proof From Food Impurity
sections.gist: Rava infers from R. Shimon's one exception that he forbids the broken-necked donkey. The Gemara answers that no one meant to eat it, which leads it to test whether a prohibition counts as intent and to look at a donkey slaughtered for practice.

children.title: Why No Exception for the Peter Chamor?
children.gist: If R. Shimon permitted benefit after *arifah*, the broken-necked donkey would be food like meat in milk, and he would have listed it as a second exception.

bullets.text: Rava: R. Shimon names only meat in milk as susceptible to *tum'at okhlin*. Had he permitted benefit from the *peter chamor* after *arifah*, the *tanna* should have said "R. Shimon concedes regarding a *peter chamor* and meat in milk."
Since the *peter chamor* is not listed as an exception, R. Shimon must hold it is *asur be'hana'ah* after its neck is broken, and so it is not food.
The list of non-food items is read as a list of things *asur be'hana'ah*. That makes it direct evidence for R. Shimon's concession.

children.title: Deflection: No Intent to Eat, and Issuro Zehu Machshavto
children.gist: The Gemara answers that the donkey isn't food because no one meant it to be eaten. The Rabbis would then call it food only because its prohibition counts as intent.

bullets.text: Had the one who broke its neck intended people to eat it, R. Shimon too would count it as food, since benefit is permitted.
The baraita is speaking of a case with no such intent, since even gentiles don't usually eat donkey meat.
Then why do the Rabbis count it as food? The Sages before Rav Sheshet: *issuro zehu machshavto*, its prohibition serves as its intent.
For *tum'at okhlin*, an item must be something people commonly eat, or else someone must have *machshavah* to eat it. On this answer the forbidden status stands in for that *machshavah*.

children.title: Testing Issuro Zehu Machshavto: Two Mishnayot and Rava's Conclusion
children.gist: Two Mishnayot require intent for carcasses that are forbidden to eat. The first is assigned to R. Shimon, but the second's closing clause is R. Shimon's own, so Rava concludes that no one holds the principle.

children.title: Kosher Bird's Carcass: Needs Machshavah, Not Hekhsher
children.gist: Teharot 1:1 requires intent before a kosher bird's carcass counts as food, though it is forbidden to eat. The Gemara assigns the Mishnah to R. Shimon.

bullets.text: Challenge from Teharot 1:1. One of the thirteen rules the Sages stated about a kosher bird's carcass is that it needs *machshavah* to become food, since most gentiles don't eat it, but it needs no *hekhsher* by contact with liquid.
It needs no *hekhsher* because the carcass can itself impart impurity. It needs *machshavah* because people don't normally eat such carcasses.
If a prohibition serves as intent, why is intent needed here? Answer: this Mishnah follows R. Shimon, who does not hold *issuro zehu machshavto*.

The roles are inverted. In the opening baraita the Rabbis went by physical edibility and R. Shimon used the prohibition to narrow what counts as food. Here the Rabbis would use the prohibition to widen it, and R. Shimon goes by what is actually eaten.

children.title: Okatzin 3:3: Carcasses, Villages vs. Marketplaces, and Kosher Signs
children.gist: This Mishnah too requires intent for forbidden carcasses. Its closing clause quotes R. Shimon on animals with some kosher signs, so its unattributed opening must be the Rabbis.

bullets.text: First clause: a non-kosher animal's carcass (horse, donkey) anywhere, and a kosher bird's carcass or a kosher animal's fat in the villages, all need intent to eat, though none needs contact with liquid.
If a prohibition serves as intent, why is intent needed? First answer: this too is R. Shimon.

The continuation: a kosher animal's carcass anywhere, and the fat in the marketplaces, need neither intent nor liquid, since they are presumed food for gentiles. By implication, a non-kosher animal's carcass does need intent.

This cannot also be R. Shimon, because the closing clause quotes him: even the camel, hare, rock badger and pig need neither intent nor liquid, since they have some kosher signs. So the unattributed first clause is the Rabbis, and they require intent for a forbidden carcass.
R. Shimon adds a new factor: how close halakha places the animal to the realm of food. An animal with one kosher sign is close enough to count without intent.

Tosafot: some non-kosher animals, the pig above all, are prized meat among gentiles. What pushes the carcass out of the category of food is the double disqualification: a non-kosher species and a carcass.

children.title: Rava: No One Says Issuro Zehu Machshavto
children.gist: Rava concludes that everyone, the Rabbis included, rejects the principle. So the Rabbis too cannot call a broken-necked donkey food without intent, and their dispute with R. Shimon needs a new explanation.

bullets.text: Rava: everyone agrees that we do not say *issuro zehu machshavto*.
So when a *peter chamor*'s neck was broken with no intent to eat it, the Rabbis too hold it is not food. What, then, do they and R. Shimon dispute?

children.title: Slaughtered for Practice: Nimos vs. R. Eliezer, or Kosher Signs?
children.gist: The Gemara sets the baraita's dispute in a donkey slaughtered only for practice, parallel to Nimos and R. Eliezer on a crow, then questions whether their dispute is about that at all.

returns_to.note: A new explanation of the dispute in Rava's baraita

children.title: A Crow Slaughtered for Practice: Its Blood, and the Crow Itself
children.gist: Both *tanna'im* say the blood of the practice slaughter is a *hekhsher*. They differ over whether the crow itself is food without intent, and R. Shimon and the Rabbis are said to differ the same way over the donkey.

bullets.text: The baraita's case: the donkey was slaughtered to teach oneself how to slaughter, not to eat. Here R. Shimon and the Rabbis disagree whether the prohibition serves as intent, as Nimos and R. Eliezer do.

R. Yosei: Nimos, brother of R. Yehoshua HaGarsi, told him that when one slaughters a crow for practice, its blood renders foods susceptible, since blood is one of the seven liquids. R. Eliezer: the blood of slaughter always renders foods susceptible.

R. Eliezer seems to say just what Nimos says. The difference must be the crow itself. Nimos requires intent to make the crow food, since people don't eat crows. R. Eliezer requires none, since its prohibition serves as intent.
Likewise with the donkey slaughtered for practice: R. Shimon requires intent, while the Rabbis treat the prohibition as intent.

children.title: Or Is the Crow Food Because of Its Kosher Signs?
children.gist: Perhaps R. Eliezer counts the crow as food because it has some kosher signs, which a donkey lacks. The practice slaughter is mentioned only because of Nimos.

bullets.text: How do we know that is their dispute? Perhaps R. Eliezer's reason is that a crow has some signs of a kosher bird. A donkey has none, so slaughtering it for practice would not make it food.
Kosher signs matter for food impurity: this is R. Shimon's reason for the camel, hare, rock badger and pig.

Then why dispute specifically a slaughter for practice? For R. Eliezer the crow should be food even if it was slaughtered unawares. Indeed it is; the case was chosen because of Nimos, who holds that even a deliberate slaughter for practice does not make the crow food.
If so, the Nimos–R. Eliezer dispute need not concern slaughter for practice, and the attempt to anchor the donkey case in it loses its support among the *tanna'im*.

children.title: The Cleaver Baraita: After Arifah, or Benefit From Value vs. Body?
children.gist: A baraita seems to have R. Shimon permit the donkey after its neck is broken. The Gemara reads both its clauses as speaking of the living donkey, one about benefit from its value and one about benefit from its body.

bullets.text: Objection to the view that R. Shimon concedes: one who does not want to redeem breaks the donkey's neck from behind with a cleaver and buries it, and it is *asur be'hana'ah*; this is R. Yehuda. R. Shimon permits.
Deflection: read it as "while alive it is forbidden" (R. Yehuda) and R. Shimon permits. R. Shimon may still concede after *arifah*.

Challenge: the latter clause already deals with the living donkey. One may not kill it with a reed, sickle, ax or saw, nor shut it in a room to starve; and shearing it or working it is forbidden (R. Yehuda), while R. Shimon permits. So the first clause must be after death.
Answer: both clauses speak of the living donkey. The first is about benefit from its value (renting or selling); the latter is about benefit from its body (shearing or labor).
Both are needed. From value alone one might think R. Shimon concedes on the body. From the body alone one might think R. Yehuda concedes on value.

children.title: Amora'im: Does R. Shimon Concede After Arifah?
children.gist: Rav Nachman brings two proofs that R. Shimon concedes, a *gezerah shavah* from the *eglah arufah* and Levi's baraita, and both are deflected. Reish Lakish agrees with him, while R. Yochanan (or R. Elazar) holds that the dispute continues after death.

children.title: Gezerah Shavah From the Eglah Arufah: R. Shimon's Source or R. Yehuda's?
children.gist: A baraita forbids the donkey after *arifah* by analogy to the *eglah arufah*. Rav Nachman says only R. Shimon would need that; Safra reads it as R. Yehuda, teaching that *arifah* doesn't work like redemption.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuh: R. Shimon concedes that after *arifah* the *peter chamor* is *asur be'hana'ah*.
Proof: a baraita links "break its neck" (Shemot 13:13) with the *eglah arufah* (Devarim 21:4). Just as the heifer is forbidden after its ceremony, so is the donkey after *arifah*.
This can't be R. Yehuda, who forbids the donkey already while alive, so no verse is needed. It must be R. Shimon.

Rav Sheshet to Rav Nachman: Safra, your colleague, explained it as R. Yehuda. *Arifah* stands in place of redemption ("if you do not redeem it, break its neck"), so one might think it permits benefit the way redemption does. The verse teaches that it does not.

children.title: 'His Money Shall Be Lost': Forbidden Carcass, Lost Difference or Death's Depreciation
children.gist: Levi's reason for *arifah*, that the owner's money is lost, seems to require R. Shimon to forbid the carcass. The Gemara explains the loss for either *tanna* without that.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman's second proof, from Levi's baraita: the owner caused the *kohen* a loss by not giving him a lamb, so his own money shall be lost.
For R. Yehuda the donkey's value was already lost while it was alive. So the baraita must be R. Shimon, and breaking the neck makes benefit forbidden.
Answer one, following R. Yehuda: the loss is the difference between the donkey's value and the cheaper lamb, which the owner would have kept had he redeemed it.
For example, a donkey worth 100 redeemed with a lamb worth 50 leaves the owner 50.
Answer two, following R. Shimon even if he permits benefit after *arifah*: death itself lowers the value, since a dead donkey is worth less than a live one.

children.title: Reish Lakish vs. R. Yochanan: Still in Dispute After Death
children.gist: Reish Lakish sides with Rav Nachman, while R. Yochanan, some say R. Elazar, holds that R. Shimon permits the donkey even after its death.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish likewise says that R. Shimon concedes the donkey is forbidden after *arifah*.
R. Yochanan, and some say R. Elazar: the matter is still in dispute. R. Shimon permits benefit even after the donkey's death.

At stake: whether *arifah* is itself an act that makes the animal forbidden, a penalty for failing to redeem, or only the procedure for an unredeemed donkey, with no effect on its status. None of the proofs settles it.

children.title: The Kiddushin Mishnah: Betrothing With a Peter Chamor
children.gist: Two versions of how the Mishnah invalidating a betrothal made with a *peter chamor* (firstborn donkey) fits the *tanna'im*: after *arifah*, when all forbid it, or per R. Yehuda with a donkey worth only a shekel. This leads to how much a *peter chamor* is redeemed for.

returns_to.note: Another version of where Rav Nachman's statement was taught

children.title: First Version: After Arifah, All Agree
children.gist: Some teach Rav Nachman's statement on this Mishnah: it speaks of a donkey after *arifah*, which even R. Shimon forbids.

bullets.text: Kiddushin 56b: one who betroths a woman with a *peter chamor*, she is not betrothed, since benefit is forbidden. Does this Mishnah exclude R. Shimon?
Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuh: it speaks of betrothal after *arifah*, when all, even R. Shimon, forbid benefit.

children.title: Second Version: A Donkey Worth a Shekel, and R. Yosei bar Yehuda's Minimum
children.gist: The Mishnah seems to fit neither *tanna*. Rav places it with R. Yehuda, for a donkey worth only a shekel, since the redemption lamb must be worth at least a shekel.

bullets.text: Others say the Mishnah fits neither *tanna*. For R. Shimon she should be betrothed with the donkey's full value. For R. Yehuda, with the difference between the donkey's value and the lamb given to the priest.
Rabba bar Avuh in the name of Rav: it is R. Yehuda, where the donkey is worth only a shekel, the same as the lamb, so no difference is left.
R. Yehuda follows R. Yosei bar Yehuda. A baraita: "you shall redeem" teaches that you redeem it immediately and for any amount; R. Yosei bar Yehuda says there is no redemption for less than a shekel.
A betrothal needs something of monetary value. With the shekel floor, a donkey worth a shekel leaves the owner nothing to give.

children.title: 'You Shall Redeem': Immediately and for Any Amount, Unlike the Firstborn Son
children.gist: The verse is needed because the *peter chamor* is juxtaposed with the firstborn son, who is redeemed at thirty days for five *sela*.

bullets.text: Isn't it obvious that the donkey may be redeemed immediately and for any amount? No: the verse sets the *peter chamor* beside the firstborn son (Bamidbar 18:15), so one might think the donkey is redeemed like the son, at thirty days and with a lamb worth five *sela* (18:16).
So "you shall redeem" teaches that the donkey is redeemed immediately after birth, and for any amount.

children.continues: Continues on 10b–11a: R. Yosei bar Yehuda's shekel is derived from "all your valuations shall be with the shekel of the Sanctuary" (Vayikra 27:25), which the Rabbis limit to one who can't afford a valuation. Rav Nachman rules like the Rabbis.

key_terms.definition: The firstborn male of a donkey, which its owner must redeem by giving a lamb to a kohen. If he does not redeem it, he must break its neck.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The daf asks whether R. Shimon, who permits benefit from it while alive, forbids it once its neck is broken, and whether a betrothal made with it is valid.

key_terms.sense: breaking the neck of an unredeemed firstborn donkey
key_terms.definition: Killing an unredeemed firstborn donkey by breaking its neck, the Torah's alternative to redeeming it. The same term is used for the heifer killed by a town's elders over an unsolved murder.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether *arifah* makes the donkey forbidden even for R. Shimon: argued from the food-impurity baraita, the cleaver baraita, a *gezerah shavah* with the *eglah arufah*, and Levi's baraita.

key_terms.definition: A status under which one may not derive any benefit from an item: not eat it, sell it, use it or feed it to animals or gentiles.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Shimon holds that items *asur be'hana'ah* are not food, since they can't be fed to others. The question is whether the broken-necked donkey is among them.

key_terms.definition: The ritual impurity that applies to foods. An item is subject to it only if it counts as food, and, in most cases, only after contact with a liquid has made it susceptible.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Whether forbidden items, carcasses and a donkey slaughtered for practice count as food for this impurity, and what makes them food: permitted benefit, a time when they were fit to eat, intent, common practice or kosher signs.

key_terms.sense: intent to eat, conferring food status
key_terms.definition: An owner's intention to eat something that people don't usually eat. It turns such an item into food for purposes of food impurity.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Carcasses that people don't commonly eat need it, and the daf asks whether a prohibition can take its place.

key_terms.sense: a prohibition to eat as a substitute for intent
key_terms.definition: The proposed principle that an item's being forbidden to eat marks it as food, so that it counts as food without anyone intending to eat it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Proposed to explain the Rabbis' view of the broken-necked donkey, it is tested against two Mishnayot. Rava concludes that no one holds it, and it returns in the Nimos–R. Eliezer dispute.

key_terms.sense: making food susceptible to impurity by contact with liquid
key_terms.definition: Food becomes susceptible to impurity only after it has been wet by one of seven liquids, among them water and blood.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The carcasses in the Mishnayot need no *hekhsher*, and the blood of a crow slaughtered for practice acts as one.

judgment_calls: The Nimos–R. Eliezer passage (10b.1–10b.8) could be its own top-level section; kept under Rava's proof because it is the Gemara's continuing attempt to explain the dispute in Rava's baraita, with a returns_to link to s3.

The cleaver baraita (10b.9–10b.14) could sit under the amora'im section, since it is an objection to the view that R. Shimon concedes; kept separate because it is a self-contained test of a tannaitic source, before the amora'im's own statements.

The Kiddushin Mishnah passage is an alternative version of where Rav Nachman's statement was taught and could nest under s13; made top-level because the second version develops into an independent discussion (the shekel minimum and the redemption derivation), with a returns_to link to s14.
Rava's conclusion (10a.12) placed with the tests of the principle rather than with the practice-slaughter answer, since it concludes those tests; its last clause sets up 10b.1.
coverage_notes: The shiur's opening minutes (the food-impurity baraita and R. Yochanan's reason) belong to 9b.21–10a.1 and are outside this scope.
The essay attributes the concession to 'Rav Nachman and Rava' and omits Reish Lakish; the text has Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuh, and Reish Lakish agreeing. Followed the text.

The Sefaria text names the author of the 10a proof 'Rava' but writes 'Rabba' at 10b.9 and 10b.15; the outline calls him Rava and avoids repeating the variant name in 10b. Worth checking against the printed text.
The essay speaks of 'Rav Sheshet Safra'; the text has Rav Sheshet telling Rav Nachman that Safra, his colleague, interpreted the baraita. Followed the text.
The essay calls the cleaver baraita 'lo ratza lishchot'; the text is 'if he does not want to redeem'. Followed the text.

The essay names 'R. Yosi b'Rabbi Yehuda' and credits the resolution to the Gemara; the text has R. Yosei bar Yehuda, and the resolution comes from Rabba bar Avuh in the name of Rav. Followed the text.
The essay ends the daf with 'teku'; the text records the amora'im's dispute without stating teiku. The outline says only that none of the proofs settles it.

In Okatzin 3:3 (10a.10) the Sefaria translation has the kosher bird carcass 'in any location' in the continuation, though the first clause requires intent for it in villages. The chart shows the clauses as the text gives them and omits the bird from the continuation row.

The essay's account of 10b.6–10b.8 ('the Gemara accepts the point') is garbled in its order; the outline follows the text: kosher signs proposed, supported from R. Shimon, and the practice-slaughter case explained as chosen because of Nimos.
